questions.stem: Why does delegating a large codebase search to a subagent help the main session's context, even though the subagent reads more files than the main agent would have?

options.text: Subagents use a cheaper model, so their tokens are not counted.
The subagent works in its own context window and returns only its conclusion, so the file contents never enter the parent's transcript.
Subagent tool results are compressed before being added to the parent context.
Subagents run after the main session ends, so there is no overlap.

questions.explanation: Context isolation is the primary architectural reason to use a subagent. The parent pays for the task description and the returned summary; the hundred file reads stay in the child's window and are discarded with it.

distractor_notes.A: Model choice affects cost, not the isolation property.
distractor_notes.C: It is not compression — the intermediate work simply never crosses the boundary.
distractor_notes.D: Subagents run within the parent's task.

analogy.text: It is why you call a service instead of importing its whole database: you get the answer across the boundary, not the working set.

questions.objective: when NOT to use a subagent
questions.stem: In which situation is a subagent the WRONG choice?

options.text: Sweeping 400 files to find every caller of a deprecated function.
A tightly interactive refactor where the parent needs the full detail of every file it touches.
Running an independent security review of a diff.
Summarising a large log file down to its distinct error signatures.

questions.explanation: Isolation cuts both ways. When the parent genuinely needs the detail, sending it to a child and getting a summary back destroys the information you needed and adds a round trip. Subagents pay off when the ratio of material examined to conclusion returned is high.

questions.stem: A team wants every session in their repository to begin with the current sprint's ticket list already in context. Which mechanism fits best?

options.text: Paste the tickets into `CLAUDE.md` and update it daily by hand.
A `SessionStart` hook that fetches the tickets and emits them as additional context.
A `PostToolUse` hook on the Read tool.
A slash command each developer must remember to run.

questions.explanation: `SessionStart` fires when a session begins or resumes and can inject dynamic context — current branch, open tickets, recent deploys — that would be stale the moment it was written into a static file.

distractor_notes.C: Fires after unrelated reads, far too late and too often.
distractor_notes.D: Depends on human memory; hooks are the deterministic layer.

analogy.text: It is the shell's `.bashrc` versus a note telling everyone to export the variable themselves.

questions.stem: An agent runs `npm test` on a suite that prints 40,000 lines on failure. What is the most effective mitigation?

options.text: Increase the context window.
Have the agent run the suite with a reporter or filter that surfaces only failures, e.g. piping through a summariser or using a compact reporter.
Ask the agent not to read the output.
Disable the Bash tool and read the test files instead.

questions.explanation: Tool output lands in context verbatim, so the cheapest fix is at the source: make the command emit less. A compact reporter, a quiet flag, or a wrapper that extracts only failing cases turns 40,000 lines into the twenty that matter.

distractor_notes.A: Buys headroom for one run and costs money on every run.
distractor_notes.C: It is already in context by then.
distractor_notes.D: Removes the ability to know whether tests pass.

analogy.text: Same principle as sampling and log levels: you do not ship DEBUG from production to your SIEM and then filter at the dashboard — you filter at the emitter.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT consume the context window?

options.text: System prompt and loaded `CLAUDE.md` files
Tool definitions for every enabled MCP server
Files on disk that the agent has not read
The full text of previous assistant turns

questions.explanation: Only what is actually placed in the request counts: system prompt, memory files, tool schemas, the transcript, and tool results. Unread files cost nothing — which is precisely why targeted retrieval is the core context discipline.

distractor_notes.B: Tool schemas are sent with each request; a dozen chatty servers can cost thousands of tokens before you type anything.
distractor_notes.D: The whole transcript is re-sent each turn.

questions.stem: A repository has 14 MCP servers enabled, and engineers report that sessions feel slow and the model sometimes picks odd tools. Select the TWO sound remedies.

options.text: Scope servers to the projects that need them rather than enabling all of them at user scope.
Disable tool descriptions to shrink the schema payload.
Consolidate overlapping servers so there is one obvious tool per job, reducing selection ambiguity.
Switch every session to a larger context window.
Instruct the model in `CLAUDE.md` to ignore the servers it does not need.

questions.explanation: Every enabled server's tool schemas are sent on every request, and near-duplicate tools make selection genuinely ambiguous. Fix both structurally: narrow scope so a project sees only its own servers, and remove overlap so each capability has one canonical tool.

distractor_notes.B: Descriptions are how the model chooses correctly; removing them makes selection worse.
distractor_notes.D: Pays money to keep the noise.
distractor_notes.E: The schemas are still sent and still cost tokens; an instruction does not unload them.

analogy.text: It is admission-webhook sprawl. Every registered webhook is consulted on every request, and two that do nearly the same thing are worse than one that does it well.

questions.stem: Anthropic's recommended agentic-coding workflow for a non-trivial change is best summarised as:

options.text: Code first, then explain the change afterwards.
Explore the relevant code, produce a plan and have it reviewed, implement, then commit with tests.
Generate ten candidate implementations and pick the shortest.
Write the commit message first and let it drive the code.

questions.explanation: Explore → plan → code → commit. The expensive mistakes are made in the first two phases, and they are also the cheapest phases to correct — which is why plan mode and an explicit human approval step exist between them.

distractor_notes.A: Skips the phase where design errors are cheap.
distractor_notes.C: Wasteful and rarely converges on quality.

analogy.text: It is design review before implementation, the same reason an RFC precedes a large PR.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude Code to never mark work complete on the basis of an unverified claim. Which `CLAUDE.md` entry best encodes that?

options.text: 'Always be accurate.'
'Before reporting a task complete, run `pnpm test` and paste the summary line; if you did not run it, say so explicitly.'
'Tests are important to this team.'
'Never make mistakes.'

questions.explanation: The instruction names the action, the command, the evidence to produce, and the fallback when it could not be done. That is a rule an agent can actually follow and a reviewer can actually check.

questions.stem: Claude Code has made several edits down a wrong path. The developer wants to return the conversation and the files to an earlier point rather than manually undoing changes. Which capability is designed for this?

options.text: `/rewind`, which restores to an earlier checkpoint in the session.
`/compact`, which drops the bad turns from context.
`/clear`, which reverts the working tree.
There is none; recover with git.

questions.explanation: `/rewind` steps the session back to an earlier checkpoint, with the option to restore code, conversation, or both. Git remains the durable safety net, but rewind handles the in-session case without leaving the tool.

distractor_notes.B: Summarises; it does not undo edits.
distractor_notes.C: Clears conversation only — files are untouched.
distractor_notes.D: Git works, but there is a purpose-built affordance.

analogy.text: Rewind is a hard reset to a checkpoint, scoped to the session, with the transcript reset alongside the tree.

questions.stem: An architect argues that improving a repository's README and module docstrings is 'AI enablement work' with measurable ROI. What is the strongest technical justification?

options.text: Agents cannot read code, only prose.
Good docs let the agent orient with a few cheap reads instead of exploratory searching, which reduces tokens, latency and the chance of building on a wrong mental model.
Documentation is cached by the provider and therefore free.
It lets the team delete their `CLAUDE.md`.

questions.explanation: Orientation cost is real and recurring: every session pays it. Documentation that answers 'what is this, where does it live, what are the rules' converts a dozen speculative searches into two targeted reads, and it happens to be the same investment that helps human newcomers.

distractor_notes.A: Agents read code fine; it is just slower and more token-hungry than reading a good summary.
distractor_notes.C: Caching is a request-level optimisation, not a property of documentation.

questions.stem: Which statement about `@` imports in memory files is correct?

options.text: Imports may nest to a bounded depth, and cycles are not expanded infinitely.
Imports are single-level only; an imported file's own imports are ignored entirely and reported as an error.
Imports may nest without limit, so a cycle will exhaust the context window.
Imports are resolved lazily at the moment the agent decides it needs the file.

questions.explanation: Nested imports are supported up to a bounded depth, which both enables composition (a root file importing team files that import module files) and prevents a cycle from being expanded forever.

distractor_notes.C: The depth bound exists precisely to stop that.
distractor_notes.D: Imports are resolved when memory is loaded.

questions.stem: Select the TWO signals that most reliably indicate a session should be cleared rather than compacted.

options.text: The developer is moving to an unrelated ticket.
The context indicator is at 80% but the current task is half done.
The agent keeps referring to a file from a previous, abandoned approach.
The last tool call returned a large diff.
The session has been open for more than an hour.

questions.explanation: Clear at a *topic* boundary: a new ticket, or contamination from an abandoned approach that keeps resurfacing. Compact when the topic is unchanged but the transcript has grown. Elapsed time and a single large tool result are not, by themselves, reasons to discard the thread.

distractor_notes.B: Textbook compaction case — same task, too much transcript.
distractor_notes.D: One big result is a compaction or filtering concern.
distractor_notes.E: Duration is a proxy at best; topic drift is the real signal.

questions.stem: Which governance practice best prevents a shared `CLAUDE.md` from decaying in a 60-engineer organisation?

options.text: Quarterly manual audits by the architecture guild.
Requiring that any PR changing build commands, test tooling or a documented invariant updates `CLAUDE.md` in the same PR, enforced by a CODEOWNERS rule and a CI check.
Locking the file so only architects can change it.
Regenerating it with `/init` every sprint.

questions.explanation: Decay happens in the gap between a change and the documentation of that change. Closing the gap inside the same PR — with ownership and an automated reminder — is the only approach that scales; audits find rot late and locking the file guarantees it.

distractor_notes.A: Detects rot up to three months after it started misleading people.
distractor_notes.C: Creates a bottleneck, so the file simply stops being updated.
distractor_notes.D: Regeneration discards the hard-won human curation that made it valuable.

analogy.text: The same reason schema migrations ship in the PR that changes the model, not in a quarterly cleanup ticket.

questions.stem: In a headless CI run, which memory sources are loaded?

options.text: None; memory is an interactive-only feature.
The same hierarchy as interactive use — enterprise, project and user memory — subject to what exists on the runner.
Only the enterprise managed policy.
Only files explicitly passed with `--memory`.

questions.explanation: Headless mode changes the interaction model, not the configuration model. The practical caveat is that an ephemeral CI runner has no `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, so behaviour can differ from a laptop — which is an argument for keeping anything CI depends on in the committed project memory.

distractor_notes.D: No such flag; discovery is hierarchical.

questions.stem: A 90-minute agent task must survive several compactions and produce a coherent final report. Which design is most robust?

options.text: One long session, relying on auto-compaction to preserve what matters.
A driver that writes findings to a structured file after each phase, with each phase starting from a fresh context that reads that file.
Ten parallel agents, merging their transcripts at the end.
One session with `/compact` run every five minutes.

questions.explanation: Make the durable artefact the source of truth and treat context as disposable working memory. Each phase then starts clean, reads the accumulated findings, does one bounded job, and appends — so no compaction can lose the result, and the final report is assembled from the file, not from recollection.

distractor_notes.A: Auto-compaction optimises for continuity, not for your report's completeness.
distractor_notes.C: Merging ten raw transcripts is a context problem, not a solution.
distractor_notes.D: Frequent lossy summarisation compounds the loss.

analogy.text: Phases are states, the findings file is the execution state, and each Lambda is stateless. That is how long workflows survive restarts — and compactions.

snippet.title: Phase driver with externalised state (Claude Agent SDK)
snippet.code:
import pathlib
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions

STATE = pathlib.Path("findings.json")

async def run_phase(name: str, instruction: str) -> None:
    prior = STATE.read_text() if STATE.exists() else "{}"
    prompt = (
        f"Prior findings:\n{prior}\n\n"
        f"Phase '{name}': {instruction}\n"
        "Append your findings to findings.json. Do not rewrite earlier entries."
    )
    async for _ in query(prompt=prompt, options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Write", "Grep"], permission_mode="acceptEdits")):
        pass
